catalog_quote: All nouns have a simple citation form and nouns in an unmarked (absolutive) position appear in that citation form. Pure, native Bantawa nouns comply with the phonological rules for syllable forms and syllabification. Except when the noun is a derivation of a verb or other category, the rather weak word stress falls on the first syllable. In case of derivations, the word stress falls on the root of the derivation. ... [p. 140] The first syllable of infinitives bears the weak word stress, realised in higher pitch and greater amplitude. Unmarked infinitives show a gradually falling pitch contour on the first syllable. ... Since Bantawa is not a tone language in general, we can assign L as the default tone to all syllables, and write L.L for normal two-syllable infinitives. Due to the stress placement, however, the normal pitch contour is HL.L, HL representing a falling contour on the norma…

audit.recode_to: (no recode; keep MORPHOLOGICAL) Add Rai 1985:34 as a second, corroborating source for default-initial stress; note in the record that (i) Rai's eastern (Rabi/Dhankuta) dialect statement is 'first syllable is always stressed in normal speech' (stress non-phonemic) and is silent on derived words, (ii) neither grammar describes stress under possessive or verbal person/negative prefixes. The fixed-dominant-vs-morphological treatment of root-initial languages is a catalog-wide policy question (Khaling coded morphological; Lango/Tewa/Kambera fixed-dominant via the register lineage), not a Bantawa-specific recode.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding passages are verbatim in the held LOT 222 text at the stated pages (p. 74 sec. 3.2.3; p. 140 sec. 4.3.7); locators correct. (2) Deciding source: Doornenbal 2009 is the standard 497-pp reference grammar and the best available description; but its stress evidence is a passing remark ('rather weak word stress' on the first syllable; derivations stress the root) with no prosody section and no examples, so the 'morphological' label rests on one unsupported sentence about derived nouns. The language does have prefixal derivation (ka- active participles, p. 184) and possessive/person prefixes, so 'root of the derivation' plausibly means non-initial stress in ka-Σ forms, which makes the morphological reading defensible; stress behaviour under possessive and verbal person prefixes is not described at all. sources.quote: 'Stress and nasalization are not phonemic in Bantawa but the first syllable is always stressed in normal speech[;] vowels preceding and following a nasal are nasalized but this is considered automatic and non-phonemic.' (Section 1.2.4 pp. 33-34 treats word juncture with minimal pairs like Taya+ma vs Tayama; no morphological conditioning of stress is mentioned anywhere in the phonology TOC.)
sources.locator: ch. 1 Phonology, section 1.2.5 'Stress and nasalization', p. 34 (PDF page = printed page)
sources.note: Second full grammar (different, eastern dialect) with an explicit phonology section on stress (1.2.5, p. 34): 'first syllable is always stressed' -- independent corroboration of default-initial stress; it does not mention the root/derivation conditioning on which our 'morphological' label rests. Only ch. 0-1 (pp. 1-55) and the TOC were fetched sources; remaining chapters are at the same handle if morphology-chapter stress remarks are wanted.

sources.note: Only other descriptive item in Glottolog's list; checked and silent on word stress (suprasegmentals = length only). Listed for completeness; adds nothing to the coding.
